2	paths: [/home/gsantos/Projects/waythrough]
3	project:
4	tags: [mcp, lsp, go, lifecycle, restart, concurrency]
5	created: 2026-08-15
6	---
7	
8	## Objective
9	
10	Add one MCP tool that restarts a named language server, so a corrupted server
11	recovers without a restart of the whole MCP session.
12	
13	## Context
14	
15	Neovim gives a user `:LspRestart`. Waythrough gives a coding agent nothing
16	like it. It restarts a server only when the process exits on its own, and it
17	stops restarting once the crash budget runs out. A server that stays alive but
18	answers from a stale index has no recovery today. The only cure is a restart
19	of the whole MCP server, which drops every other language server too.
20	
21	Waythrough cannot see that a server answers wrongly. The agent is the only
22	judge, so the recovery must be a tool the agent calls.
23	
24	## Model
25	
26	Today `Failed` is terminal: the supervisor goroutine returns, and nothing owns
27	the process any more. After the change, `Restart` re-enters `Starting` from
28	both `Ready` and `Failed`.
29	
30	Before:
31	
32	```mermaid
33	stateDiagram-v2
34	    [*] --> Starting: Start spawns the supervisor
35	    Starting --> Ready: readiness gate passes
36	    Starting --> Failed: crash budget spent
37	    Ready --> Starting: process exits, unrequested
38	    Failed --> [*]: supervisor returns, no owner left
39	```
40	
41	After:
42	
43	```mermaid
44	stateDiagram-v2
45	    [*] --> Starting: Start spawns the supervisor
46	    Starting --> Ready: readiness gate passes
47	    Starting --> Failed: crash budget spent
48	    Ready --> Starting: process exits, unrequested
49	    Ready --> Starting: Restart stops it, crash budget untouched
50	    Failed --> Starting: Restart re-supervises, crash budget cleared
51	```
52	
53	The graceful stop opens a window. The old process can still speak while the
54	new attempt starts, so every readiness signal must carry the generation that
55	produced it.
56	
57	```mermaid
58	sequenceDiagram
59	    participant Tool as restart_server
60	    participant Sup as supervisor loop
61	    participant Old as old process
62	    participant New as new process
63	
64	    Tool->>Old: shutdown, exit, kill after grace
65	    Old->>Sup: process exited
66	    Sup->>Sup: beginAttempt, generation N+1, status Starting
67	    Sup->>New: spawn, then handshake
68	    Old->>Sup: late $/progress end, generation N
69	    Note over Sup: must do nothing, or the tool reports ready too early
70	    New->>Sup: readiness gate passes, generation N+1
71	    Sup->>Tool: ready
72	```
73	
74	## Done when
75	
76	- `restart_server` exists as an MCP tool.
77	- A call on a running server returns only after the replacement passes its own
78	  readiness gate.
79	- A call on a server that already reached `Failed` does the same.
80	- A `get_definition` call that follows a restart answers from the new process.
81	- A test against `fakelsp` proves the old process ended and a new one serves.
82	- A test proves an explicit restart does not spend the crash budget.
83	- A test proves a late readiness signal from a retired attempt cannot mark the
84	  new attempt ready.
85	- A test proves a `Shutdown` that runs at the same time as a restart leaves no
86	  live subprocess behind.
87	
88	## Tasks
89	
90	- [ ] Tag readiness state with a generation, captured at spawn and carried by
91	      `client`, so `markReady`, `markFailed`, `tokenCreated` and `tokenClosed`
92	      from a retired attempt do nothing
93	- [ ] Split a graceful `stopProcess(ctx, grace)` out of
94	      `serverProcess.shutdown`, and make it return at once when the current
95	      attempt never spawned a process
96	- [ ] Keep the process-lifetime context in `Start`, and spawn every restart
97	      on it, never on the caller's context
98	- [ ] Add an instance-log flag to `fakelsp` that appends one line per process
99	      start, carrying the pid
100	- [ ] Add `Manager.Restart(ctx, name)` for a running server: stop it, let the
101	      supervisor begin a fresh attempt, then wait for the new readiness gate.
102	      The supervisor skips the crash-budget append on a requested stop, because
103	      `exits` is a local that only a new goroutine clears
104	- [ ] Re-supervise a `Failed` server on restart, with exactly one supervisor
105	      goroutine per server at every moment
106	- [ ] Put the `shuttingDown` read and the spawn decision under one lock hold,
107	      so no attempt can begin after `Shutdown` started
108	- [ ] Add the `restart_server` MCP tool, and make the unknown-server error
109	      list the configured names
110	- [ ] Update the tool list in `README.md`, and the request-flow and readiness
111	      sections in `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`
112	
113	## Scope
114

## Objective

Add one MCP tool that restarts a named language server, so a corrupted server
recovers without a restart of the whole MCP session.

## Context

Neovim gives a user `:LspRestart`. Waythrough gives a coding agent nothing
like it. It restarts a server only when the process exits on its own, and it
stops restarting once the crash budget runs out. A server that stays alive but
answers from a stale index has no recovery today. The only cure is a restart
of the whole MCP server, which drops every other language server too.

Waythrough cannot see that a server answers wrongly. The agent is the only
judge, so the recovery must be a tool the agent calls.

## Model

Today `Failed` is terminal: the supervisor goroutine returns, and nothing owns
the process any more. After the change, `Restart` re-enters `Starting` from
both `Ready` and `Failed`.

Before:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Starting: Start spawns the supervisor
    Starting --> Ready: readiness gate passes
    Starting --> Failed: crash budget spent
    Ready --> Starting: process exits, unrequested
    Failed --> [*]: supervisor returns, no owner left
```

After:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Starting: Start spawns the supervisor
    Starting --> Ready: readiness gate passes
    Starting --> Failed: crash budget spent
    Ready --> Starting: process exits, unrequested
    Ready --> Starting: Restart stops it, crash budget untouched
    Failed --> Starting: Restart re-supervises, crash budget cleared
```

The graceful stop opens a window. The old process can still speak while the
new attempt starts, so every readiness signal must carry the generation that
produced it.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Tool as restart_server
    participant Sup as supervisor loop
    participant Old as old process
    participant New as new process

    Tool->>Old: shutdown, exit, kill after grace
    Old->>Sup: process exited
    Sup->>Sup: beginAttempt, generation N+1, status Starting
    Sup->>New: spawn, then handshake
    Old->>Sup: late $/progress end, generation N

    New->>Sup: readiness gate passes, generation N+1
```

- A test proves a late readiness signal from a retired attempt cannot mark the
  new attempt ready.
- A test proves a `Shutdown` that runs at the same time as a restart leaves no
  live subprocess behind.

      `client`, so `markReady`, `markFailed`, `tokenCreated` and `tokenClosed`
      from a retired attempt do nothing

      `serverProcess.shutdown`, and make it return at once when the current
      attempt never spawned a process

      on it, never on the caller's context

      start, carrying the pid
- [ ] Add `Manager.Restart(ctx, name)` for a running server: stop it, let the
      supervisor begin a fresh attempt, then wait for the new readiness gate.
      The supervisor skips the crash-budget append on a requested stop, because
      `exits` is a local that only a new goroutine clears
- [ ] Re-supervise a `Failed` server on restart, with exactly one supervisor
      goroutine per server at every moment
- [ ] Put the `shuttingDown` read and the spawn decision under one lock hold,

# Restart lifecycle hazards in internal/lsp

Read from `internal/lsp/manager.go` and `internal/lsp/client.go` at commit
`b0a4a83`. Line numbers are from that state of the code.

The manager already restarts a server whose process exits on its own. An
explicit restart reuses that machinery, so it inherits every hazard below.
Three of these hazards exist today: H1, H2 and H6. Each one needs a narrow
coincidence to appear. An explicit restart makes all three ordinary.

## H1 — a retired attempt can mark the new attempt ready

`markReady` (manager.go:703) guards on `status != StatusStarting` only. It
does not ask which attempt is speaking. `beginAttempt` (manager.go:593) sets
the status back to `StatusStarting`. Two callers left over from the previous
attempt can then reach `markReady`. Each one marks the new server ready
before that server has indexed anything:

- `negotiateReadiness` (spawned at manager.go:184) sleeps out
  `progressDebounce`, then calls `markReady` at manager.go:675.
- `tokenClosed` (manager.go:692) runs from the old process's jsonrpc2 reader.
  `client` holds the `*serverProcess` and nothing else (client.go:17), so a
  late `$/progress` `end` from the dying process reaches the live proc.

A crash restart rarely hits this. The new process spawns milliseconds after
the old one dies, and the debounce is 250 ms. An explicit restart hits it
every time, because the graceful stop takes as long as the server needs to
answer `shutdown` and `exit`.

The headline promise then breaks. `restart_server` reports ready. The agent's
next `get_definition` reaches a server that is still indexing.

`markFailed`, `tokenCreated` and `tokenClosed` have the same blind spot.

### Guard shape

Give `serverProcess` a generation counter. Bump it in `beginAttempt`.
Capture it where each caller starts:

| Caller | Captures the generation at |
| --- | --- |
| `negotiateReadiness` | the `go` statement in `runServer` |
| `client` | `protocol.NewClient` in `startProcess` (manager.go:624) |

Then `markReady`, `markFailed`, `tokenCreated` and `tokenClosed` take the
generation and return without effect when it does not match. This is the
invariant the restart feature rests on, and it belongs in the same family as
the checks in [[2026-08-15-invariant-checks-and-coverage-gate]].

## H2 — a failed spawn leaves exitedCh open forever, and shutdown blocks on it

`startProcess` assigns `p.cmd` only after `cmd.Start()` succeeds
(manager.go:619-629). `runServer` calls `proc.wait()` only inside the
`err == nil` branch (manager.go:182-187), and `wait` is the only writer that
closes `exitedCh` (manager.go:743).

Take a spawn that fails on an attempt that is not the first. Two things hold
after it:

- `p.exitedCh` is the fresh channel `beginAttempt` made, and no one will ever
  close it.
- `p.cmd` still holds the previous attempt's finished `exec.Cmd`. That value
  is not nil.

`shutdown` (manager.go:752) reads both. `cmd != nil`, so it does not take the
early return. It waits on `exited`, times out after `killGrace`, kills a
process that already finished, and then waits on `<-exited` at
manager.go:776 with no timer left. That wait never ends.

The existing test at manager_test.go:217 covers `cmd == nil`, which is the
case where the command never existed at all. It does not reach this one.

Today the path needs a binary that works once and then disappears. With an
explicit restart, an agent that restarts a server after a toolchain rebuild
walks straight into it. The graceful-stop primitive that restart needs is a
split of this same function, so the fix belongs to the same slice.

## H3 — re-supervising a Failed server skips beginAttempt

`runServer` calls `beginAttempt` only when `attempt > 0` (manager.go:178).
The comment explains why: `NewManager` already built the first
`readyCh`/`exitedCh` pair, so the first attempt must not replace it.

A restart of a `Failed` server has no supervisor goroutine to signal, because
`runServer` returned after `markFailed` (manager.go:201-204). It needs a new
goroutine. That goroutine starts at `attempt == 0`, so it skips
`beginAttempt`. Three pieces of dead state survive:

- `status == StatusFailed`, so `WaitReady` returns `failed to start`
  immediately, forever (manager.go:238).
- `readyCh`, closed by `markFailed` (manager.go:722), so no waiter can ever
  block on it again.
- `openFiles`, still holding the dead server's document versions, so
  `syncFile` sends `didChange` to a server that never saw a `didOpen`.

Constraint: before any waiter observes a re-supervised server, its status is
`StatusStarting` and its `readyCh` is a fresh open channel. Reaching that
means `runServer` cannot read "first attempt ever" from `attempt == 0`.

## H4 — the spawning context owns the child process

`startProcess` uses `exec.CommandContext(ctx, ...)` (manager.go:608), and
that `ctx` comes from `Start`. `internal/cli/serve.go:57-58` passes
`context.Background()` on purpose, so the language servers outlive any single
MCP session.

A restart arrives on an MCP tool call. The harness cancels that call's
context when the tool returns. A spawn on it kills the new server the moment
the agent gets its answer.

The manager must keep the process-lifetime context it received in `Start`,
and spawn every restart on that one. The caller's context is still the right
context for the ready-wait timeout, and for nothing else.

## H5 — fakelsp cannot show that the process changed

A restart test must prove that the old process ended, and that a different
one now serves. `fakelsp` offers only `-crash-marker`
(fakelsp/main.go:38), which fires once and then stays quiet.

An append-only instance log, one line per process start, gives a test a
direct reading. The test counts the lines, and compares the pid before and
after.

## H6 — Shutdown can race a restart and leave an orphan process

`Manager.Shutdown` copies the proc list (manager.go:468-472), then calls
`serverProcess.shutdown` on each entry. That function takes `p.mu`, sets
`shuttingDown`, and reads `cmd` and `exitedCh` (manager.go:753-758).

`runServer` reads the same flag through `shutdownRequested` (manager.go:189),
just after `proc.wait()` returns. The flag read and the spawn that follows
take the lock twice, with a gap between them. A stop that lands in that gap
produces this order:

1. Something stops the old process. `wait` closes generation N's `exitedCh`.
2. `runServer` reads `shuttingDown` as false, and loops.
3. `Shutdown` sets `shuttingDown`, and reads generation N's `exitedCh`, which
   already closed. It returns at once, and reports success.
4. `runServer` runs `beginAttempt` and spawns generation N+1.

`serve` then returns while the new child runs. `exec.CommandContext` holds the
process-lifetime context from serve.go:58, which nothing cancels, so nothing
reaps that child. The subprocess outlives `waythrough serve`.

A crash that coincides with `Shutdown` reaches this order today. The window is
one flag read wide. An explicit restart widens it to the whole graceful stop,
which lasts as long as the server needs to answer `shutdown` and `exit`.

Constraint: one lock hold must cover both the `shuttingDown` read and the
decision to spawn. A `Shutdown` that starts first wins. A `Shutdown` that
starts second still stops the attempt that began while it ran.

13	// inherited from protocol.UnimplementedClient.

22	// so this request is the only path a server has to start reporting, which
23	// keeps the readiness gate's token tracking complete.
24	func (c *client) WorkDoneProgressCreate(
25		ctx context.Context,
26		params *protocol.WorkDoneProgressCreateParams,
27	) error {
28		c.proc.tokenCreated(tokenKey(params.Token))
29		return nil
30	}
31	
32	// Progress records when a token the server opened closes. The readiness
33	// gate does not need "begin" or "report": a token counts as open from the
34	// moment it is created until its "end" arrives.
35	func (c *client) Progress(ctx context.Context, params *protocol.ProgressParams) error {
36		var value struct {
37			Kind string `json:"kind"`
38		}
39		if err := json.Unmarshal([]byte(params.Value), &value); err != nil {
40			return nil
41		}
42		if value.Kind == "end" {
43			c.proc.tokenClosed(tokenKey(params.Token))
44		}
45		return nil
46	}

49		data, err := protocol.Marshal(token)
50		if err != nil {
51			return ""
52		}
53		return string(data)
54	}

29		}

41		if err != nil {
42			return err
43		}
44		if err := config.Validate(cfg); err != nil {
45			return err
46		}
47	
48		absConfigPath, err := filepath.Abs(configPath)
49		if err != nil {
50			return fmt.Errorf("resolve %s: %w", configPath, err)
51		}
52		root := filepath.Dir(absConfigPath)
53	
54		// The language-server subprocesses live for as long as serve runs, not
55		// for as long as any one MCP session does: only Shutdown below ends
56		// them, never the signal-aware context the MCP transport listens on.
57		manager := lsp.NewManager(root, cfg.LanguageServers)
58		if err := manager.Start(context.Background()); err != nil {
59			return err
60		}

# Architecture

This document describes the file layout of Waythrough, and how a
request flows through the code. Read
[CONTRIBUTING.md](../CONTRIBUTING.md) first for how to set up your
tools and check a change.

## File layout

| Path | Content |
| --- | --- |
| `cmd/waythrough/` | The `main` package. It only calls `cli.Execute`. |
| `internal/cli/` | The `waythrough` command-line interface: `init`, `validate`, and `serve`. |
| `internal/config/` | The `waythrough.yaml` schema, plus its `Load` and `Validate` functions. |
| `internal/lsp/` | Process lifecycle for each configured language server, and the LSP client that talks to it. |
| `internal/lsp/fakelsp/` | A small language server built only for `internal/lsp` tests. |
| `internal/editor/` | The MCP server. It turns each MCP tool call into an LSP request, and the LSP response back into MCP output. |
| `scripts/` | `check.sh`, the check script, and `install-git-hooks.sh`, the hook installer. |
| `.github/workflows/` | The CI workflow and the release workflow. |
| `.tools/` | A gitignored directory. It holds the pinned `golangci-lint` binary. |
| `.goreleaser.yaml` | The GoReleaser config for the release build and the Homebrew tap. |
| `waythrough.yaml` | An example config file, used when you run Waythrough from this repository. |

## How a request flows

1. A coding agent starts `waythrough serve` over stdio, as an MCP
   server.
2. `internal/cli` loads and validates `waythrough.yaml`, through
   `internal/config`.
3. `internal/cli` starts an `internal/lsp` manager. The manager
   starts one subprocess per configured language server, and waits
   for each one to become ready.
4. `internal/cli` builds the MCP server from `internal/editor`. This
   step registers the `get_definition`, `list_references`,
   `rename_symbol`, `signature_help`, and `get_diagnostics` tools.
5. The MCP server serves tool calls until the agent's session ends.
   `internal/editor` routes each call, by the file extension in the
   call, to the language server that handles it. It sends the LSP
   request through the `internal/lsp` manager, and it turns the LSP
   response into the tool's output shape.
6. When `serve` exits, it shuts down every language server the
   manager started.

## Readiness

An LSP server's process can start before the server can answer a
request. `internal/lsp` gates on one of two readiness signals, set
per server in `waythrough.yaml`:

- `progress` — the default. The manager waits for every LSP
  `workDoneProgress` token the server opens to close.
- `handshake` — an opt-in for a server with no background indexing.
  The manager treats the server as ready as soon as the
  initialize and initialized handshake completes.

## Add a language server

Add an entry to `waythrough.yaml`. You need no code change. See the
`language_servers` schema in `internal/config/config.go`.

## Add an MCP tool

Add the tool to `internal/editor/editor.go`, and add the LSP call it
needs to `internal/lsp/manager.go`. Add tests at both levels: an
`internal/lsp` test against `fakelsp`, and an `internal/editor` test
for the tool's input and output shape.

21	
22	Waythrough publishes binaries for Linux and macOS. This project is

24	
25	```sh
26	brew tap gustavofsantos/waythrough https://github.com/gustavofsantos/waythrough
27	brew install waythrough
28	```
29	
30	## Quick start
31	
32	1. Create a `waythrough.yaml` file in your project root. Each entry
33	   names a language server, the command that starts it, and the file
34	   extensions it handles:
35	
36	   ```yaml
37	   language_servers:
38	     - name: gopls
39	       command: gopls
40	       args: []
41	       filetypes:
42	         .go: go
43	   ```
44	
45	   Run `waythrough init` to write a starter config for Clojure
46	   instead. Edit it for your own language servers. Then run
47	   `waythrough validate` to check the file for errors.
48	
49	2. Add Waythrough as an MCP server in your coding agent's config.
50	   Pass an absolute path to `--config`, so Waythrough finds
51	   `waythrough.yaml` no matter where the agent starts it from. The
52	   agent starts Waythrough over stdio:
53	
54	   ```json
55	   {
56	     "mcpServers": {
57	       "waythrough": {
58	         "command": "waythrough",
59	         "args": ["serve", "--config", "/absolute/path/to/waythrough.yaml"]
60	       }
61	     }
62	   }
63	   ```
64	
65	3. Ask your coding agent to find a definition or list references. The
66	   agent calls Waythrough's MCP tools. Waythrough forwards the
67	   request to the language server for that file type.
68	
69	## Tools
70	
71	Waythrough exposes these MCP tools to a connected coding agent:
72	
73	- `get_definition` — find where a symbol's definition is, given a
74	  file position.
75	- `list_references` — find every place that uses a symbol, given a
76	  file position.
77	- `rename_symbol` — build the list of edits that rename a symbol,
78	  across every file it touches. It does not write the edits to disk.
79	  Your agent applies them.
80	- `signature_help` — list the signatures a call could match, given a
81	  file position inside that call. It also says which signature and
82	  which parameter the position is on.
83	- `get_diagnostics` — list the problems a language server finds in a
84	  file. The language server must advertise pull diagnostics at its
85	  handshake. One that does not fails the call with an error naming it,
86	  rather than reporting a clean file. `gopls` pushes its diagnostics
87	  by default and advertises no pull support, so it fails this call
88	  today.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Validation gate for waythrough: formatting, vet, lint, build, module
# tidiness, and tests. This is the single source of truth run by both the
# local pre-commit hook (scripts/install-git-hooks.sh) and CI
# (.github/workflows/ci.yml) so the two never disagree.
set -uo pipefail

REPO_ROOT="$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel 2>/dev/null)" || {
	echo "not a git repository" >&2
	exit 1
}
cd "$REPO_ROOT"

# Keep this in sync with .github/workflows/ci.yml.
GOLANGCI_LINT_VERSION="v2.6.2"
TOOLS_BIN="$REPO_ROOT/.tools/bin"
GOLANGCI_LINT="$TOOLS_BIN/golangci-lint"

if [ -t 1 ]; then
	RED=$'\033[0;31m'; GREEN=$'\033[0;32m'; YELLOW=$'\033[0;33m'; BOLD=$'\033[1m'; NC=$'\033[0m'
else
	RED=""; GREEN=""; YELLOW=""; BOLD=""; NC=""
fi

failures=()

pass() { printf '%s✓%s %s\n' "$GREEN" "$NC" "$1"; }
fail() { printf '%s✗%s %s\n' "$RED" "$NC" "$1"; failures+=("$1"); }

# Installs a pinned golangci-lint into a repo-local, gitignored bin dir
# rather than requiring it on $PATH, so local runs and CI use the exact
# same binary and never drift.
ensure_golangci_lint() {
	if [ -x "$GOLANGCI_LINT" ] && "$GOLANGCI_LINT" version 2>/dev/null | grep -q "${GOLANGCI_LINT_VERSION#v}"; then
		return 0
	fi
	echo "${YELLOW}Installing golangci-lint ${GOLANGCI_LINT_VERSION} into ${TOOLS_BIN}...${NC}" >&2
	mkdir -p "$TOOLS_BIN"
	if ! GOBIN="$TOOLS_BIN" go install "github.com/golangci/golangci-lint/v2/cmd/golangci-lint@${GOLANGCI_LINT_VERSION}"; then
		return 1
	fi
}

echo "${BOLD}Running validation checks in ${REPO_ROOT}${NC}"
echo

# 1. Formatting
unformatted="$(gofmt -l . 2>&1)"
if [ -n "$unformatted" ]; then
	echo "$unformatted"
	fail "gofmt (run: gofmt -w .)"
else
	pass "gofmt"
fi

# 2. Vet
if vet_out="$(go vet ./... 2>&1)"; then
	pass "go vet"
else
	echo "$vet_out"
	fail "go vet"
fi

# 3. Lint
if ensure_golangci_lint; then
	if lint_out="$("$GOLANGCI_LINT" run ./... 2>&1)"; then
		pass "golangci-lint"
	else
		echo "$lint_out"
		fail "golangci-lint"
	fi
else
	fail "golangci-lint (could not install ${GOLANGCI_LINT_VERSION})"
fi

# 4. Build
if build_out="$(go build ./... 2>&1)"; then
	pass "go build"
else
	echo "$build_out"
	fail "go build"
fi

# 5. Module tidiness
if tidy_out="$(go mod tidy -diff 2>&1)"; then
	pass "go mod tidy"
else
	echo "$tidy_out"
	fail "go mod tidy (run: go mod tidy)"
fi

# 6. Tests
if test_out="$(go test ./... -race -count=1 2>&1)"; then
	echo "$test_out"
	pass "go test"
else
	echo "$test_out"
	fail "go test"
fi

echo
if [ "${#failures[@]}" -eq 0 ]; then
	echo "${GREEN}${BOLD}All checks passed.${NC}"
	exit 0
fi

echo "${RED}${BOLD}${#failures[@]} check(s) failed:${NC}"
for f in "${failures[@]}"; do
	echo "  - $f"
done
exit 1

Acceptance test written, and it fails for the right reason: `unknown tool "restart_server"`.

**Slice plan** (from the issue's "Done when"):

| # | Slice |
|---|---|
| 1 | Restart a running server (tool + `Manager.Restart` + generation guard + `stopProcess` split) |
| 2 | Restart a server that already reached `Failed` |
| 3 | A requested restart never spends the crash budget |
| 4 | `Shutdown` racing a restart leaves no live subprocess |
| 5 | Docs (`README.md`, `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`) |

**Acceptance test for slice 1** — `internal/editor/restart_server_test.go`:

**Promise 1: "answers the next question from a new server session, not the old one"**
1. `get_definition` works, so the first server is up.
2. `restart_server{"server":"fake"}` succeeds and answers `{"server":"fake","status":"ready"}`. The output shape is the contract: the call must not return until the replacement can answer.
3. `get_definition` works again and returns the same location.
4. The `-sync-log` holds **two** `didOpen@1` entries.

Step 4 is the discriminating assertion. `fakelsp` refuses a question about a document it never received, and `didOpen` at version 1 only happens on a session that knows nothing yet. A survivor process would have received `didChange@2`, and a restart that left `openFiles` behind would have sent one.

**Promise 2: "says which names it could have used"**
A call naming `gopls` fails, and the error text holds both `"gopls"` and `fake`. This answers the issue's Q2: an agent recovers the right name from the error instead of guessing.

Two notes on what I deliberately left out of this acceptance test:

git add -A internal/ && git commit -q -F - <<'EOF'
feat(lsp): restart one language server on request

A corrupted language server had no cure but a restart of the whole MCP
session, which drops every other server too. Waythrough cannot see that a
server answers from a stale index, so the agent is the only judge, and the
recovery has to be a tool it calls.

Restart stops the named server and returns once the replacement has passed
its own readiness gate. The graceful stop leaves the retired process able
to speak while the new one starts, so every readiness signal now carries
the attempt that produced it and the signals from a retired attempt are
dropped. Without that, the tool would report ready and the agent's next
request would reach a server still indexing.

The supervisor now parks instead of returning when a server spends its
crash budget, so exactly one goroutine owns a server at every moment and
every process, restarts included, spawns on the lifetime context Start was
given rather than on a tool call's own.
